newsitem.title: CAMEROON: Cameroon election attracts opposition ire.
newsitem.headline: Cameroon election attracts opposition ire.

text.p: As voters in the Cameroon capital's Tsinga district cast ballots in Chief Thomas Bomba's home in this month's election, five portraits of President Paul Biya gazed down at them from the walls.

Bomba is one of many traditional chiefs, all fervent Biya supporters, called on by the interior ministry to help organise the elections. Cameroon has no independent electoral commission to oversee the process.
"There are too many strangers, too many opposition supporters in my district," Bomba, 70, told Reuters.

By strangers he means the dynamic Bamileke from West Cameroon's overpopulated highlands, whom he has seen moving in great numbers into Tsinga, buying the best plots of land and building spacious shops and villas.

Biya's ruling Cameroon People's Democratic Movement (RDPC) won in Bomba's polling station with 149 against 146 votes for the opposition. But 323 of the 619 people registered were unable to vote: they had received no registration card, or had a card but could not find their names on the lists.

While the state-owned Cameroon Tribune reported provisional results giving the RDPC 114 out of 180 seats, most private newspapers carried complaints of fraud by distribution of voting cards and say their results show an absolute majority of 97 seats for the opposition Social Democratic Front (SDF) of John Fru Ndi.
GOVERNMENT DENIES ELECTION PROBLEMS

"I think it's all relative because no country has ever organised elections without problems. The Cameroonian people are the supreme judge and the people are serene," Communications Minister and government spokesman Augustin Kontchou Kouomegni told Reuters.

Kontchou denied reports three people were killed in a clash between opposition and ruling party supporters in Kumbo, in the south-west of Cameroon, the only place where serious unrest has been reported.
"I already have some reports, including reports from some international observers, which indicate that these elections went basically well," he said.

He denied local authorities had stopped opposition supporters in main cities getting their cards. "Many people register but don't collect their card in time. These are the growing pains of democracy," he said.
At the University of Yaounde, lecturers and students stood around the campus in small groups, discussing the vote.
"It's a scandal. Many people couldn't vote. These elections are making matters worse," said a senior lecturer.
But few expect widespread unrest once the official results are proclaimed by the Supreme Court, which has until June 6 to do so.
"I don't think people will mix work and politics again," said lawyer Petit Jean Otse Mbida at the main employers association GICAM (Groupement Inter-Patronal du Cameroun).
"Anyone who still has a job is too afraid of losing it. There won't be any sabotage of the economy, people have understood that it doesn't change the political situation."

In 1991 Cameroon lived through months of strikes, demonstrations and violence to force multi-party democracy on Biya. But presidential elections in 1992 were condemned by international observers as widely flawed, and violent demonstrations led the government to place Fru Ndi and his supporters under house arrest and declare a state of emergency in North West Province for three months.
WRITER WARNS OF REBELLION
Pro-opposition writer Mongo Beti firmly believes if the government proclaims a ruling party victory, rebellion similar to that led by Laurent Kabila in ex-Zaire is around the corner.
"If the government keeps to these results, there will be a Kabila in Cameroon in the next two to three years. Young Cameroonian exiles will organise a rebellion from former Zaire," he told Reuters.
Cameroon expects presidential elections toward the end of the year. More is at stake in those polls because it is the president who holds most power.

Asked if he would work with Cameroon's second main opposition party, the National Union for Democracy and Progress (UNDP) of Bello Bouba Maigari, SDF leader John Fru Ndi said: "You can't trust him, he is dishonest."
As in 1992, it will most likely be a divided opposition that will try to take power from Biya, who has ruled Cameroon since 1982.
"It'll be a walkover," said Kontchou, laughing, when asked about the chances of Biya, 64, winning another five-year term.
For Chief Bomba at least, this is good news. "I'm supporting the president. You know, a traditional chief should always support his president!"
